_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season10-bible-v1.0.1.md row a10e07, writer brief a10e07-v1.0.0.md, LATENT catalog v1.0.78 and latent-syllabus-v1.0.3.md. a10e06's next field was honoured (it appeared while this case was being written): an aircraft-wing factory's night shift, and splitting one model across several graphics cards: splitting each layer, giving each card a run of layers (option 2 and the explanation), and spreading a model's experts (explanation only). The title is kept as a metaphor only (one beat: four voices in two rooms); no choir, church or cathedral, no flights, passengers or runway, no oven, autoclave or furnace. Shared given data: Llama 3.1 70B, 70.6 billion weights, 80 layers, 141 billion bytes in 16 bits (141.2), about 132 GB on the card's meter (131.5 in 1,024-units); NVIDIA H100 3.35 TB/s (3,350 GB/s), NVLink 900 GB/s; sizes in the meter's units, speeds in the maker's. The factory's own measurements, never a source's: 12 ms to read a card's quarter (10.5 ms in theory, 35.3 / 3,350), a swap 0.02 ms inside a machine and 0.2 ms across the 25 Gb/s network, a hand-over the same, with one group of answers in a step or two. Story arithmetic (all in sims/a10e07-v1.0.0.js): one 4-card machine 12 + 160 x 0.02 = 15.2 ms, 66 a second, 800 tokens in 12.2 s; two 2-card machines, every swap across, 12 + 160 x 0.2 = 44 ms, 22.7 a second (the dashboard's 23), 35.2 s, waiting 73%; reply 0 two groups in each step: 44 ms each, 45.5 a second in all, 35.2 s; reply 1 another provider's 4-card machine at $4.29 against $3.99: 0.30 x 4 x 730 = $876 a month more ($12,527 against $11,651); reply 2 each card a quarter of the layers: 4 x 12 + 0.02 + 0.2 + 0.02 = 48.24 ms, 48.2 ms, 20.7 a second, 38.6 s, waiting 75%; reply 3 two ways inside each machine, half the layers each: 12 + 80 x 0.02 = 13.6 ms a stage, 2 x 13.6 + 0.2 = 27.4 ms, 36.5 a second, 21.9 s, waiting 56% with one group and 12% with two (73 a second in all); card time 4 x $3.99 = $15.96 an hour, $0.16 a check tonight, $0.05 before. One deliberate change from the brief: the brief's reply 2 counted all 3 hand-overs as crossing the network (4 x 12 + 3 x 0.2 = 48.6 ms, 20.6 a second); on two 2-card machines only the hand-over from card 2 to card 3 crosses, so the case uses 48.2 ms and 20.7 a second. The sim, like the brief's 27.4 ms, leaves out the chosen token's trip back to the first stage; the limits say so. Board: the catalog lists the concept id pipeline for this case, but that id belongs to a3e01 (a chain of programs, a different idea), so the board has no pipeline card and teaches pipeline parallelism under the parallelism card. Timeline: launch Monday 2 March 2026 on one 4-card machine; a check at 00:30 on Tuesday 22 September took 12.2 s; the provider's email Monday 14 September; maintenance from 18:00 Monday 28 September to Monday 19 October; the move done by 21:00 Monday 28 September, one untimed test question; the shift from 22:00; Berhane's check at 00:30 Tuesday 29 September, 35.2 s; Wuraola phoned Zdravko, who timed a swap at 01:00; the post at about 04:00; the fix live for the 22:00 shift on Tuesday 29 September, checks at 00:30 on Wednesday 30 September. Cold case: 1 month later, 29 September to 29 October 2026: the machine back on Monday 19 October with the 2 x 2 settings kept; at 00:30 on Tuesday 27 October the check took 21.8 s (2 x 13.6 + 0.02 = 27.22 ms, 36.7 a second); four ways inside one machine again gives 15.2 ms and 12.2 s. Standards note conditional, not legal advice. Sources read 16 October 2026.
title: A Choir in Many Rooms

post.author: u/panel_check_wuraola
post.title: I check aircraft wing panels at night. Our assistant kept the same model, cards and settings, and tonight it wrote at a third of its speed.

blocks.text: I'm Wuraola, night quality inspector at Ardvane Aerostructures, which builds aircraft wings. Overnight we check each finished panel, a curved sheet of wing skin, against its drawing.
Our assistant writes each panel's check from the drawing and our notes: about 800 tokens, the small pieces of text a language model writes. Since launch on Monday 2 March, checks took 12 s.
Ours is Llama 3.1 70B: 70.6 billion learned numbers, called its weights, at two bytes each. That's 141 billion bytes, about 132 GB, billions of bytes.
It runs on rented graphics cards, cards for short: chips of tiny adding units fed numbers along one fast memory road. One NVIDIA H100 card holds 80 GB, too little alone.
Since launch, four H100s have sat in one machine, a rented computer at our provider, the company we rent from, for $3.99 a card hour.
Each token passes through 80 layers, rounds of sums done in order. Zdravko in IT split it like one recipe shared across four benches: each card holds a quarter of every layer.
For each layer, every card works its quarter, then the four swap partial results: each sends its part, waits for the others, and adds them up. Twice per layer: 160 swaps a token.
Engineers call this tensor parallelism. Inside our machine the cards swap over NVLink, a short link carrying 900 GB a second.
The model writes in steps: each step gives every answer one more token. In a step each card reads its 35.3 billion bytes at 3,350 GB a second: 10.5 ms, thousandths of a second, in theory.
Zdravko measured 12 ms at launch, and a swap at 0.02 ms: 12 ms + 160 swaps × 0.02 ms = 15.2 ms a token, 66 tokens a second.

On Monday 14 September the provider emailed Zdravko: our machine goes for yearly maintenance from 18:00 on Monday 28 September to Monday 19 October, with no four-card machine free. It lent us two 2-card machines, same price, on its ordinary network: 25 Gb/s, billions of bits a second, about 3 GB a second.
Zdravko moved the model by 21:00 with the same settings file, every layer still split four ways. A test question came back right. Nobody timed it.

At 00:30 Berhane waited 35 seconds for a rivet-pattern check and called over: was the assistant broken? Our dashboard, the assistant's page of records, shows each check: date, time, machines, speed, length, time taken.

22 Sep 00:30  1 machine × 4 cards   66 tokens/s  800 tokens  12.2 s
29 Sep 00:30  2 machines × 2 cards  23 tokens/s  800 tokens  35.2 s
Four voices in two rooms, and before every note each one stopped to hear the others.

diagram.aria: Wuraola's drawing of two 800-token rivet-pattern checks at 00:30, timed from the moment each was asked. Top row, Tuesday 22 September on one machine: reading weights for 9.6 seconds, then waiting on swaps until 12.2 seconds. Bottom row, Tuesday 29 September on two machines: reading weights for 9.6 seconds, then waiting on swaps until 35.2 seconds, 25.6 seconds of waiting. Markers at 12.2 seconds and 35.2 seconds, each check done.

blocks.caption: Drawn at 02:00 from the dashboard. Each row adds up one check's time by kind, not in the order it happened: reading weights, 800 steps × 12 ms = 9.6 s on both nights; waiting on swaps, 800 tokens × 160 swaps × 0.02 ms = 2.6 s last week and 800 tokens × 160 swaps × 0.2 ms = 25.6 s tonight. Same 800 tokens, same model, same reading. The dashboard rounds 22.7 tokens a second to 23.

blocks.text: I phoned Zdravko, who timed a swap between the machines at 01:00: 0.2 ms, ten times the old one. The provider's network test reads 25 Gb/s, as sold.

By hand: 12 ms + 160 swaps × 0.2 ms = 44 ms a token, 22.7 tokens a second, 35 s a check. The cards read 12 ms and wait 32 ms. At $15.96 an hour for four cards, reading or waiting, a check costs $0.16, against $0.05 before.
Zdravko blames the provider's network: nothing changed on our side. Our machine is away three more weeks. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing on your inspection floor is haunted, though four cards waiting on each other in the dark is a grim picture. Your 15.2 ms was the gap between one token and the next for each answer, the inter-token latency, ITL for short (a10e02). Two questions. Tonight, how many of a token's 160 swaps travel between the two machines, and why? And while a swap is on the network, what are the cards doing, and what is their meter doing?

replies.author: u/panel_check_wuraola
replies.text: All 160. A swap needs all four cards, and two sit in each machine, so every swap goes out over the network and back. While it travels the cards sit idle. The meter runs at $15.96 an hour either way.

comments.author: u/same_settings_zdravko
comments.text: I moved it. Same cards, four H100s, same model, same settings file: I didn't change a number. If it's three times slower, the provider's network is broken, and I've asked them to fix the cable. Until they do, pack more answers into each step. Every trip between machines then carries more work, so the slow trips pay for themselves. That settings file has run cleanly since March; I'm not rewriting it in the middle of the night for a cable fault.

replies.author: u/panel_check_wuraola
replies.text: The provider's network test reads 25 Gb/s, as sold.

replies.author: u/same_settings_zdravko
replies.text: Then someone else's traffic is on our cable. Either way, it isn't our settings.

comments.author: u/quarter_each_mulugeta
comments.text: Day-shift stress engineer. Why split a layer at all? Give each card a quarter of the layers instead, 20 each. Card one runs layers 1 to 20 and hands its one result to card two, which runs layers 21 to 40, and so on down the line. That's 3 hand-overs a token instead of 160 swaps, and only one of them crosses the network. Engineers call splitting by layers pipeline parallelism.

replies.author: u/panel_check_wuraola
replies.text: While card two runs its layers, what are cards one, three and four doing?

replies.author: u/quarter_each_mulugeta
replies.text: Waiting their turn. But they'd be waiting on 3 hand-overs, not 160 swaps.

comments.author: u/works_manager_seppo
comments.text: Another provider has a four-card machine free this week at $4.29 a card hour against our $3.99. That's $1.20 an hour more, $876 a month at that rate, until ours comes back. An inspector's hour costs more than that. I'd sign today.

replies.author: u/panel_check_wuraola
replies.text: Our customers' panel drawings would sit with a second company, under a second contract.

replies.author: u/works_manager_seppo
replies.text: Then the quality office reads the contract this morning. That's what it's for.

reply.prompt: It's 04:00 on Tuesday 29 September. Our machine is away until Monday 19 October, and the next shift starts at 22:00 tonight. What should Ardvane change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Send more answers in each step so every swap across machines does more.
options.verdict: More in each trip, the same wait
options.part2: On Tuesday afternoon Zdravko set the program to put the night's questions into two groups that share every step, and left the four-way split alone. The provider's engineers checked the cable that afternoon and found nothing wrong. At 00:30 on Wednesday Berhane asked for a rivet-pattern check again. Each swap now carried both groups' partial results and still took about 0.2 ms, because nearly all of it is the trip, not the load. In the sim: 44 ms a token for every answer, 22.7 tokens a second each, 45.5 a second in all. Berhane's check took 35.2 s, the same as the night before. The night's checks still ran at a third of September's speed, and the cards still spent 73% of their paid time waiting.
options.senior: Packing more answers into each step raises the total, 45.5 tokens a second against 22.7, but not the speed any one inspector sees. Each swap still makes the trip between machines, 160 times a token, and on this network a trip costs about 0.2 ms whether it carries one group's partial results or two: each answer's share is a small parcel of numbers, and the wait is the trip. The fault is the number of crossings, not their size. And the cable was never broken: 25 Gb/s is what the provider sold.

options.text: Rent a four-card machine from another provider until ours returns.
options.verdict: Fast again, at $876 a month more
options.part2: The quality office read the second provider's terms on Tuesday morning and agreed that our drawings could go there for three weeks (their reading of the contract, not legal advice). Seppo signed at noon. By 20:00 Zdravko had moved the model, every layer split four ways inside one four-card machine again, and handed the two lent machines back to our provider. At 00:30 on Wednesday Berhane's check came back in 12.2 s: 15.2 ms a token, 66 a second. The bill: $4.29 instead of $3.99 a card hour, $1.20 an hour more, $876 a month at that rate, until our machine returned on 19 October. And our customers' panel drawings now sat with a second company, under a second contract the factory has to watch as closely as the first.
options.senior: An honest trade. Putting all four cards back behind one fast link restores the old speed, because every swap stays inside the machine: 12 ms + 160 × 0.02 ms = 15.2 ms. It costs $0.30 a card hour more, a second supplier holding the drawings, and a second move when ours returns. And it fixes tonight, not the lesson: the next time the cards are spread over machines, the same settings file will send every swap over the slow network again.

options.text: Give each card a quarter of the layers, so no layer is split at all.
options.verdict: No swaps, and three cards idle
options.part2: On Tuesday Zdravko gave each card 20 layers. For each token, card one ran layers 1 to 20 and handed its result to card two inside the first machine; card two handed across the network to card three; card three handed to card four inside the second machine. No swaps at all, three hand-overs. At 00:30 on Wednesday Berhane's check took 38.6 s, longer than the night before. In the sim: 4 × 12 ms + 0.02 + 0.2 + 0.02 ms = 48.2 ms a token, 20.7 tokens a second. Each card read for 12 ms and then waited 36 ms for the other three: 75% of every paid hour spent waiting, and the night's checks ran slower than ever.
options.senior: Splitting by layers removes the swaps but runs the four quarters one after another, so a token takes four cards' reading time, 48 ms, instead of one card's 12. Each card is idle three-quarters of the time unless several groups of answers are in flight to fill the gaps, and even then each inspector's own answer still takes 48.2 ms a token. A split by layers pays across a slow link, with as few stages as there are machines; inside a machine, with a fast link, splitting every layer keeps all the cards working on every token.

options.text: Split layers only inside a machine; give each machine half the layers.
options.part2: On Tuesday afternoon Zdravko changed two numbers in the settings file: each layer split two ways, between the two cards inside one machine, and the layers split in two, 1 to 40 on the first machine and 41 to 80 on the second. Now for each token the first machine runs its 40 layers, its pair of cards swapping 80 times over their own fast link, then hands one result across the network; the second machine runs the rest. In the sim: 12 ms + 80 × 0.02 ms = 13.6 ms for each machine's stage, 2 × 13.6 + 0.2 ms = 27.4 ms a token, 36.5 tokens a second. The program kept two groups of answers in flight, so while the second machine worked on one group the first worked on the other: each card waited 12% of the time instead of 73%. At 00:30 on Wednesday Berhane's check came back in 21.9 s. Same machines, same $3.99 a card hour, the drawings with the same provider. Checks still took about 10 s longer than in September while our machine was away.
options.senior: Match the split to the links. Splitting a layer costs two swaps per layer, so keep it where the link is fast, inside a machine; splitting by layers costs one hand-over per token at each boundary, so put that boundary on the slow link. vLLM's own guide says the same: set the tensor split to the cards per machine and the pipeline split to the number of machines. Tonight 160 swaps cross nothing and one hand-over crosses the network. The price of the layer split is the bubble: with one group of answers each machine idles while the other works, 56% of its time, so keep two groups in flight. It will not match one four-card machine, 27.4 ms against 15.2, but it uses the machines you have at the price you pay.

sim.title: Plan the split for Ardvane's two lent machines
sim.lede: You're Wuraola at 00:29:50 on Tuesday 29 September, ten seconds before Berhane's rivet-pattern check. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: Llama 3.1 70B, 80 layers, 141 billion bytes of weights, a quarter on each of four H100 cards, 35.3 billion bytes each; an H100's memory road moves 3,350 GB a second, so a quarter takes 10.5 ms in theory. The factory's own measurements, never a source's: reading a quarter takes 12 ms a step, with one group of answers in the step or two; a swap or a hand-over takes 0.02 ms inside a machine and 0.2 ms across the provider's 25 Gb/s network, with one group or two. A split layer needs two swaps; a check is 800 tokens. Prices per card hour, close to one provider's list: ours $3.99, another provider's four-card machine $4.29; a month is 730 hours. The sim, like the story, leaves out the chosen token's trip back to the first machine.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the opening view is tonight: two 2-card machines, every layer split four ways, 160 swaps across the network, 44 ms a token, a check in 35.2 s, 73% of card time waiting. Play 00:30. Switch to one 4-card machine and see 15.2 ms. Back on two machines, try two groups of answers: more tokens in all, no faster for Berhane. Give each card a quarter of the layers. Then split two ways inside each machine with half the layers each, with one group and then two. Play each reply. Last, put that two-by-two split on one 4-card machine and compare it with four ways.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the inspection floor was haunted. The settings file split every layer four ways, so each token needs 160 swaps among all four cards. On one machine each swap took 0.02 ms over the fast link; on two lent machines every swap crossed the 25 Gb/s network at 0.2 ms: 12 ms + 160 × 0.2 ms = 44 ms a token instead of 15.2 ms, and the cards spent 32 ms of every 44 waiting.

steps.title: One token, 80 layers, four cards.
steps.text: Llama 3.1 70B's weights take 141 billion bytes, about 132 GB on the meter, and an H100 holds 80 GB, so the model must be split. First, each card is given a quarter of the weights, 35.3 billion bytes. Second, for every token, each card reads its quarter along its memory road: 35.3 billion bytes ÷ 3,350 GB a second = 10.5 ms in theory, 12 ms on the factory's own measurement. Third, the cards' work is combined into the next token. How it is combined is the split, and the split decides how often the cards must talk. A machine here is one rented computer in the provider's building, as in Dead Letter's s1e10: cards inside one machine share a fast link, and machines share a slower network. What can go wrong: treating four cards as one big card, wherever they sit.

steps.title: Tensor parallelism: split every layer, swap twice per layer.
steps.text: First, every card works its quarter of a layer. Second, all four swap partial results: each sends its part, waits for the others, and adds them up; engineers call this an all-reduce. Third, the same happens again for the layer's second half, and then the next layer starts. The Megatron-LM paper split layers this way with only two all-reduces in the forward path of each layer: 80 layers × 2 = 160 swaps a token. All four cards work on every token, which is why it is fast, but no card can move on until every swap is done. Inside one machine: 12 ms + 160 × 0.02 ms = 15.2 ms, 66 tokens a second. Across two machines every swap crosses the network: 12 ms + 160 × 0.2 ms = 44 ms, 22.7 a second. A swap carries a small parcel of numbers, so nearly all of its 0.2 ms is the trip itself; two groups of answers in each step still leave each answer at 44 ms. What can go wrong: 160 short waits a token, cheap on a short link and ruinous on a long one.

steps.title: Pipeline parallelism: give each machine a run of layers.
steps.text: First, the first machine runs layers 1 to 40, its two cards splitting each layer and swapping over their own fast link: 12 ms + 80 × 0.02 ms = 13.6 ms, one stage. Second, it hands its one result across the network, 0.2 ms. Third, the second machine runs layers 41 to 80, another 13.6 ms stage. A token takes 2 × 13.6 + 0.2 = 27.4 ms, 36.5 tokens a second, a check in 21.9 s. The catch is the bubble: with one group of answers, each machine sits idle while the other works, 56% of its paid time. With two groups in flight, one in each machine at once, waiting falls to 12% and the pair writes 73 tokens a second in all. Giving each of the four cards a quarter of the layers removes every swap but runs four 12 ms readings one after another: 4 × 12 ms + 0.24 ms of hand-overs = 48.2 ms, 20.7 a second. What can go wrong: a pipeline with one group in flight, or more stages than there are slow links to cross.

steps.title: Expert parallelism: for models built from experts.
steps.text: Some models, called mixture-of-experts models, replace part of each layer with many smaller blocks called experts, and each token uses only a few of them. First, each card holds some of the experts. Second, each token travels to the cards holding its experts. Third, the results travel back and are combined. DeepSeek's EPLB notes that the load of different experts may vary depending on the current workload, so it duplicates heavy-loaded experts onto more cards. Llama 3.1 70B uses every weight for every token, so it has no experts to spread; this is the third kind of split a serving team meets. What can go wrong: one popular expert's card becomes the queue every token waits in.

steps.title: Why it never showed, and the sum by hand.
steps.text: Since launch on Monday 2 March the model had never left one machine, so the four-way split always swapped over the fast link. Nothing in the settings file says where the cards sit. The provider's maintenance on Monday 28 September carried the same file onto two machines, and one test question checked that the model answered, not how fast. By hand: four cards at $3.99 an hour cost $15.96 an hour; tonight's check used 35.2 s of them, $0.16, against $0.05 last week, and 32 ms of every 44 ms went on waiting. What can go wrong: a placement change treated as no change, because no number in the settings file moved.

diagram.aria: Two ways to place Llama 3.1 70B on two 2-card machines. Top row, tonight: machine 1 holds cards 1 and 2, a quarter of every layer each; 160 swaps a token all cross the network at 0.2 ms; machine 2 holds cards 3 and 4; 44 ms a token, 22.7 tokens a second, 73% waiting. Bottom row, the fix: machine 1 runs layers 1 to 40 in a 13.6 ms stage; one hand-over crosses the network, 0.2 ms; machine 2 runs layers 41 to 80 in 13.6 ms; 27.4 ms a token, 36.5 tokens a second, 12% waiting with two groups.

notes.text: Tonight: every layer split 4 ways across 2 machines
The fix: split inside each machine, half the layers each
Each card reads its 35.3 billion bytes in 12 ms

explain.caption: Read each row left to right. Tonight every layer is split across all four cards, so each of a token's 160 swaps needs cards in both machines and crosses the network. The fix keeps each layer's swaps inside one machine and sends one hand-over a token across the network.

fix.title: The fix: split each layer only inside a machine, and give each machine half the layers
fix.text: While the lent machines are in use, change the settings file to split each layer two ways, between the two cards inside one machine, and to give each machine half the layers, 1 to 40 and 41 to 80. Keep two groups of answers in flight so neither machine waits on the other. Then time it on our own checks before the shift: 27.4 ms a token, a check in about 22 s. Write down which split goes with which placement, and treat any move of the cards as a change that gets timed again, not only a test question that comes back right. When the cards sit in one machine again, the rule gives one machine and every layer split four ways inside it.

limits: The 12 ms reading and both swap times are the factory's own measurements, not a source's. A real swap takes longer as more answers and more cards share it, so measure your own link before you plan on it.

The two-by-two split is slower than one four-card machine, 27.4 ms against 15.2 ms, and it needs two groups of answers in flight to keep both machines busy; with one inspector asking at a time, each card waits 56% of its paid time. The sim also leaves out the chosen token's trip back to the first machine and the program's own overheads.

Expert parallelism applies only to mixture-of-experts models. For a model like Llama 3.1 70B, the choice is between splitting each layer and splitting by layers, and how to place each on the links you have.

explain.seniorTake: A model too big for one card must be split, and the split decides how often the cards talk. Splitting every layer, tensor parallelism, puts all the cards to work on every token, at the price of two swaps per layer, 160 a token here: cheap over a fast link inside a machine, ruinous over a network where each one waits 0.2 ms. Splitting by layers, pipeline parallelism, talks once per boundary per token, but runs the stages one after another and leaves each idle unless several groups of answers are in flight. So match the split to the links: split each layer where the link is fast, hand over between machines where it is slow; vLLM's guide puts it as the tensor split to the cards per machine and the pipeline split to the number of machines. Mixture-of-experts models add a third split, by expert, with its own trouble: busy experts must be copied. A settings file that describes the split says nothing about where the cards sit, so a placement change is a change, and it gets timed on your own answers. The meter runs while the card waits: 32 ms of every 44 was paid waiting.

realWorld.title: Megatron-LM: two all-reduces a layer
realWorld.text: Shoeybi and colleagues' Megatron-LM paper splits each layer across cards using only two all-reduces in the forward path and two in the backward path. Serving only runs forward, so a split layer costs two swaps: 160 for Llama 3.1 70B's 80 layers.

realWorld.title: Megatron-LM: fast inside, slower between
realWorld.text: Their cluster had 300 GB/sec bandwidth between GPUs inside a server via NVSwitch and 100 GB/sec of interconnect bandwidth between servers using 8 InfiniBand adapters per server, and in their set-up two or more GPUs within the same server form model parallel groups. Those are their training cluster's figures, far faster than the provider's 25 Gb/s network.

realWorld.title: vLLM: one machine, then several
realWorld.text: vLLM's Parallelism and Scaling guide says that if the model is too large for a single GPU but fits on a single node with multiple GPUs, use tensor parallelism, and if the model is too large for a single node, combine tensor parallelism with pipeline parallelism. A node is what the story calls a machine.

realWorld.title: vLLM: the sizing rule
realWorld.text: The same page says: Set tensor_parallel_size to the number of GPUs per node and pipeline_parallel_size to the number of nodes. On two 2-card machines that is 2 and 2, the senior answer. It adds: Efficient tensor parallelism requires fast internode communication, preferably through high-speed network adapters such as InfiniBand.

realWorld.title: H100: the road and the link
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's H100 page gives the H100 SXM 80GB of GPU memory, a GPU memory bandwidth of 3.35TB/s, and NVIDIA NVLink at 900GB/s. 141 billion bytes do not fit on one card, and a quarter of them takes 10.5 ms to read in theory.

realWorld.title: DeepSeek EPLB: copying busy experts
realWorld.text: DeepSeek's Expert Parallelism Load Balancer says that when using expert parallelism (EP), different experts are assigned to different GPUs, and because the load of different experts may vary depending on the current workload, they adopt a redundant experts strategy that duplicates heavy-loaded experts.

realWorld.title: What the cards cost
realWorld.text: Lambda's pricing page, read on 16 October 2026, lists the NVIDIA H100 SXM at four prices from $3.99 to $4.29 per GPU per hour by machine size, plus applicable taxes. The story's $3.99 and $4.29 are given data close to that list, not Lambda's price for any machine in the story: 4 cards × 730 hours × $0.30 = $876 a month. Prices change; the arithmetic is the lesson.

asked: Explain tensor and pipeline parallelism, and when you would use each.
How would you serve a 70B model on two 2-GPU machines?
interview.answer: Both split a model that is too big for one GPU; they differ in how often the GPUs must talk. Tensor parallelism splits every layer: each GPU computes its share, then all of them all-reduce their partial results, twice per layer, so an 80-layer model does 160 all-reduces per token. Every GPU works on every token, so it is fast, but only over a fast link like NVLink inside one machine. Pipeline parallelism gives each GPU or machine a run of layers and hands one result to the next stage per token, so it tolerates a slow link, but the stages run in turn, and with one batch in flight each stage idles while the others work: the bubble. You fill it with several batches in flight. On two 2-GPU machines I'd run tensor parallel size 2 inside each machine and pipeline parallel size 2 across them, as vLLM's docs recommend, and keep at least two groups of requests in flight. On a 25 Gb/s network that took one example from 44 ms a token with 4-way tensor across machines to 27.4 ms, against 15.2 ms on one 4-GPU machine. Then I'd time it on real requests after every placement change, because the settings file doesn't know where the GPUs are. For mixture-of-experts models there's a third option, expert parallelism, where you also watch for hot experts and replicate them.

terms.def: The parts that make up an aircraft's frame: wings, panels, ribs. Ardvane Aerostructures builds wings.
A curved sheet of wing skin, riveted to the frame. Night inspectors check each finished one against its drawing.
Where the rivets go on a panel and how far apart. A rivet-pattern check compares the panel with its drawing.
The assistant's written check list for one panel, about 800 tokens, from the drawing and the inspectors' notes.
One of the inspectors who check finished panels overnight. Wuraola and Berhane are two.
A program that writes text one small piece at a time, having learned from huge amounts of text (a1e01).
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads and writes (a1e03). A panel check is about 800.
The learned numbers a model is made of (a1e02). Llama 3.1 70B has 70.6 billion, two bytes each in 16 bits.
Meta's open-weights language model with 70.6 billion weights in 80 layers: 141 billion bytes in 16 bits, about 132 GB on a card's meter.
A byte holds 8 bits. A GB is about a billion bytes, a TB a thousand GB. Speeds use the maker's 1,000; the card's meter counts 1 GB as 1,024 MB.
Billions of bits a second, a network's speed. 25 Gb/s is about 3 GB a second, against NVLink's 900 GB a second.
Short for graphics card: a board with a GPU, chips of small adders, and its own memory (a10e01). Ardvane rents four.
The card Ardvane rents: 80 GB of memory, a memory road of 3,350 GB a second, and NVLink to the other cards in its machine at 900 GB a second.
This season's word for the link that carries the weights from the card's memory to its adders (a10e01). Its speed sets the shortest step.
One rented computer in the provider's building, holding one or more cards. Cards inside a machine share a fast link; machines share a slower network.
The company Ardvane rents its machine from, at $3.99 a card hour. It lent two 2-card machines during its yearly maintenance.
The provider taking a machine out of service to service it. Ardvane's went away from 18:00 on Monday 28 September to Monday 19 October 2026.
One of the rounds of sums a model runs every token through, in order (a10e01). Llama 3.1 70B has 80.
How a model too big for one card is shared across several: each layer split among cards, or each card or machine given a run of layers, or both.
One card's share of a split layer's answer. The cards' partial results must be added together before the layer can go on.
Each card sends its partial result, waits for the others' parts, and adds them up. A split layer needs two. 0.02 ms inside a machine, 0.2 ms across the network here.
The engineers' name for a swap: every card sends its part, and every card ends up with the sum of all the parts.
Splitting every layer across cards, so all the cards work on every token, with two swaps per layer. Fast over a fast link, slow over a slow one.
NVIDIA's short, fast link between the cards inside one machine: 900 GB a second on the H100.
The cables and switches joining the provider's machines. Ardvane's lent machines are joined at 25 Gb/s, about 3 GB a second.
One pass of writing: each card reads its weights once and every answer in the step gets one more token (a10e04).
A millisecond, a thousandth of a second. A token took 15.2 ms on one machine and 44 ms on two.
The file that tells the serving program how to split the model, such as every layer four ways. It says nothing about where the cards sit.
The assistant's page of records: one line per check, with the date and time, the machines, the speed, the length and the time taken.
The gap between one token and the next for an answer: one step (a10e02). 15.2 ms on one machine, 44 ms on two.
In a split by layers, one stage sending its one result to the next. 0.02 ms inside a machine, 0.2 ms across the network here.
Splitting by layers: each card or machine runs a run of layers and hands one result to the next, like stations on a line. One hand-over per boundary per token.
One link in a split by layers: the card or machine that runs one run of layers. In the fix each machine is a 13.6 ms stage.
The idle time in a split by layers, when a stage has nothing to do while the others work. Filled by keeping several groups of answers in flight.
Answers written together in one step. With two groups, one stage works on one while the next stage works on the other.
The share of paid card time a card is not reading its weights: waiting on swaps, hand-overs or another stage. 73% on Monday night.
What the cards cost while a job runs: four cards at $3.99 an hour cost $15.96 an hour, reading or waiting.
A kind of model that replaces part of each layer with many smaller blocks, called experts, and sends each token through only a few of them.
Splitting a mixture-of-experts model by expert: each card holds some experts and tokens travel to the cards holding theirs. Busy experts may be copied.
DeepSeek's Expert Parallelism Load Balancer, which copies heavy-loaded experts so no card carries far more than the rest.
A paper by Shoeybi and colleagues at NVIDIA (2019) that splits each layer across GPUs with only two all-reduces in the forward path.
What joined the GPUs inside a server in Megatron-LM's cluster, at 300 GB/sec between them.
What joined the servers in Megatron-LM's cluster: 100 GB/sec between servers, using 8 InfiniBand adapters per server.
What vLLM's guide calls a machine: one computer holding several cards.
A free, widely used serving engine for language models (a10e04). Its guide sets the tensor split to the cards per machine and the pipeline split to the number of machines.
The international standard for information security management. Its Annex A lists controls, such as 8.32 change management and 5.23 cloud services.
Making sure changes to systems are assessed, approved, tested and recorded before they go live. Annex A 8.32.
Annex A 5.23: how an organisation acquires, uses, manages and leaves cloud services, such as rented machines.

atWork: Look for a model served across several cards whose split was written for one machine: a tensor split of 4 or 8 typed once at launch and carried along when the cards moved, for a provider's maintenance, a cheaper region or a bigger cluster. It is a common pattern: the settings stay the same, the model answers correctly, and every swap now crosses a slow network. Ask four things. Which cards share each layer, and do they sit in one machine? How many swaps does a token need, and how long does one take on the link between those cards? With a split by layers, how many groups of answers are in flight, and how much of each stage's paid time is waiting? And after the last move, did anyone time the model on real requests, or only check that it answered? A later build project will ask you to measure this. Standards-readiness note, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, an auditor checking Annex A 8.32 (change management, as summarised by a third-party guide) would look for a re-test after a placement change, such as a timed replay of real requests before the shift, and one checking Annex A 5.23 (information security for use of cloud services) would look for the provider's maintenance terms and an agreed plan for where the model runs while a machine is away. As they apply to you; this is not legal advice.

recall.prompt: Your team serves a 70B model on one rented 8-GPU server, every layer split eight ways. For a week the cloud moves you onto two 4-GPU servers joined by an ordinary network, with the same settings. Answers now come at a third of their old speed, and the network test passes. What happened, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Splitting every layer needs two swaps (all-reduces) per layer among all the GPUs; with the GPUs in two servers, every one of them now crosses the slow network
Split each layer only among the GPUs inside one server and give each server a run of layers (tensor parallelism within, pipeline parallelism across)
Keep several groups of requests in flight so neither server idles (the bubble), and re-time the model after any placement change

recall.model: Nothing broke; the placement changed. Splitting every layer eight ways means two all-reduces per layer among all eight GPUs, and with four GPUs in each server every one of them now crosses the network between the servers, at many times the cost of the fast link inside one. The fix is to split each layer only within each server, four ways over its fast link, and give each server a run of layers, half the layers each, with one hand-over a token between the servers: tensor parallelism inside, pipeline parallel across, as vLLM's guide recommends. Keep at least two groups of requests in flight so neither server sits idle in the bubble while the other works, and re-time the model on real requests after any placement change, since the settings never say where the GPUs sit.

recall.prompt: Each of four cards reads its quarter of the weights in 12 ms, and every layer is split four ways: 160 swaps a token. With the cards in two machines, a swap takes 0.2 ms. How long does one token take?
recall.why: 12 ms of reading plus 160 swaps × 0.2 ms = 32 ms of waiting: 44 ms, 22.7 tokens a second. 15.2 ms is the same split inside one machine, where a swap takes 0.02 ms; 32 ms is the waiting alone.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: explain tensor and pipeline parallelism, and when you would use each.

keyIdeas.idea: Tensor parallelism splits every layer across GPUs, so all work on every token, but they all-reduce partial results twice per layer and need a fast link
Pipeline parallelism gives each GPU or machine a run of layers with one hand-over per token at each boundary; stages run in turn, so several groups must be in flight to fill the bubble
Use tensor parallelism inside a machine and pipeline parallelism between machines: tensor size to GPUs per machine, pipeline size to the number of machines

recall.model: Both split a model too big for one GPU. Tensor parallelism splits every layer: each GPU computes its share, then they all-reduce partial results, twice per layer, so every GPU works on every token, but only a fast link like NVLink keeps those all-reduces cheap. Pipeline parallelism gives each GPU or machine a run of layers and hands one result over per token at each boundary, which a slow link can carry, but the stages run in turn, so you keep several groups in flight to fill the bubble. Use tensor parallelism inside a machine and pipeline parallelism between machines: vLLM's guide sets the tensor size to the GPUs per node and the pipeline size to the number of nodes. On two 2-GPU machines on a slow link that took a 70B model from 44 ms a token to 27.4 ms.

recall.prompt: A mixture-of-experts model is served with expert parallelism, each card holding some experts. One expert becomes far busier than the rest tonight, and its card holds everyone up. What does DeepSeek's EPLB do about it?
options: Spreads all the weights evenly across the cards
Duplicates the heavy-loaded experts onto more cards
Sends each token through every expert
Moves the busy expert to the slowest card
recall.why: EPLB notes that the load of different experts may vary with the workload and duplicates heavy-loaded experts, so their tokens are shared across copies. Splitting every layer is tensor parallelism; sending every token through every expert would undo the point of experts.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 1 month later. From the Tuesday night shift on 29 September the assistant ran split two ways inside each lent machine, half the layers each, with two groups in flight: checks in about 22 s. Our machine came back from maintenance on Monday 19 October, and Zdravko moved the model onto it that evening, with the new settings file, "the one that fixed it". On Tuesday 27 October at 00:30 Berhane's rivet-pattern check took 21.8 s, on the machine that used to do it in 12. The dashboard says 36.7 tokens a second, with all four cards back in one machine on NVLink. Zdravko says the old machine must have come back slower.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does the check still take about 22 s back on the four-card machine, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: On one machine every link is fast, so the split by layers only costs: the two halves run one after the other, and each pair of cards idles while the other works (27.2 ms a token)
Split every layer four ways inside the one machine again (tensor parallelism): 15.2 ms a token, a check in about 12 s
Choose the split from the placement each time (tensor size to cards per machine, pipeline size to the number of machines) and re-time after every move

coldCase.model: The machine isn't slower; the split is now wrong for it. The two-by-two settings were right for two machines on a slow network, where each layer's swaps had to stay inside a machine. On one machine every link is fast, so the split by layers only costs: the two halves run one after the other, 13.6 ms each plus a 0.02 ms hand-over, 27.2 ms a token, and each pair of cards sits idle while the other half works unless two groups are in flight. Split every layer four ways inside the one machine again, tensor parallelism over NVLink: 12 ms + 160 × 0.02 ms = 15.2 ms a token, a check in about 12 s. And pick the split from the placement every time, the tensor split to the cards per machine and the pipeline split to the number of machines, which here is one, then re-time it on real checks after every move.
